edits.find: Night blindness has a short differential and the fundus settles it in one look. Optic disc pallor with attenuated retinal vessels and patchy pigmentary change is the triad of retinitis pigmentosa — rods degenerate first, and rods are densest in the midperiphery and responsible for dim-light vision, which is why the first symptom is night blindness and the first field defect is midperipheral. Acuity stays 20/20 until cones go late. Every competing option is excluded by a finding the examiner deliberately printed: a normal red reflex and 20/20 vision close cataract, a pale rather than cupped disc closes glaucoma, a two-month progressive course with no tear closes detachment, and normal cornea and conjunctivae close vitamin A deficiency, whose ocular disease is xerophthalmia.

Hyporeflexia is a lower motor neuron sign, which localises at or below the anterior horn cell and eliminates spastic diplegia outright, since cerebral palsy is by definition an upper motor neuron disorder. Three findings then pick the lesion: bladder involvement, because muscle and peripheral nerve diseases spare the bladder; back pain, which points at a structural spinal lesion; and pes cavus, which is chronic denervation of the intrinsic foot muscles.

One lesion sits upstream of all four systems: a tethered cord from closed spinal dysraphism, stretched by two months of growth.

edits.find:
The stem hands you Reye syndrome and then refuses to offer it as an answer. Viral prodrome → "over-the-counter medications" (the aspirin, never named) → a biphasic course (better, then vomiting and lethargy) → hepatomegaly without splenomegaly → cerebral edema. But the question asks for the cause of the imaging finding, so it steps one level down, to mechanism.

Every option can cloud consciousness. Only one causes edema. Ammonia entering astrocytes is combined with glutamate into glutamine by glutamine synthetase. Glutamine is osmotically active and cannot leave — water follows, astrocytes swell, and you get cytotoxic cerebral edema. Hypoglycemia, uremia and adrenal crisis produce encephalopathy by other routes and leave the brain the same size.

Adrenal insufficiency: plausible until you read the blood pressure. Hypothyroidism: nobody fell for it, because the pulse and temperature contradict it in the same line.

edits.find:
A stroke in a teenager is never "just a stroke": the question is what made the artery fail. Two findings decide it here. Weeks of fever, weight loss and aches say systemic inflammation. Unequal pulses or arm pressures say several large arteries are narrowed at once. Inflammation plus multiple fixed large-artery stenoses is a large-vessel vasculitis, and in an adolescent that is Takayasu arteritis.

The exception is endocarditis. It also brings fever and stroke, but emboli occlude one vessel at a time and never narrow the aorta's branches, so the pulses stay equal. Look for the murmur and the embolic skin findings instead.
